title: Forging and rolling: shaping hot and cold metal by squeezing
examples: What is the difference between hot and cold working?
Why are forged parts stronger than cast parts?
How does a rolling mill reduce thickness?

parts.label: Top roll R 250 mm
parts.ask: How does a rolling mill reduce thickness?

explain.say: A blacksmith hammering a red-hot bar is forging. A steelworks squeezing a slab between giant rollers into sheet for cars is rolling. Both shape metal in the solid state by pushing it. Look at the rolling mill: a 10 millimetre slab enters between two rolls and leaves as an 8 millimetre strip.

draw.text: Forging and rolling: shaping hot and cold metal by squeezing

parts.label: Top roll R 250 mm
parts.ask: How does a rolling mill reduce thickness?

explain.say: Metal does not change volume as it deforms. So if the thickness drops from 10 to 8 millimetres with the width the same, the strip must come out longer and faster: 10 over 8, which is 1.25 times. In at 1 metre per second, out at 1.25. See the strip leaving faster?

parts.label: Top roll R 250 mm
parts.ask: How does a rolling mill reduce thickness?

explain.say: How big a bite can the rolls take? Friction must drag the slab in. The maximum draft, the thickness drop per pass, is mu squared times roll radius. With mu 0.12 and a 250 millimetre radius, that is 3.6 millimetres. Our 2 millimetre draft is fine. What would happen if you tried a 5 millimetre bite?

parts.label: Top roll R 250 mm
parts.ask: How does a rolling mill reduce thickness?

explain.say: The rolls would just skid on the slab! Now temperature matters. Hot working, above the recrystallisation temperature, needs low force and allows big changes, because new grains keep forming. Cold working near room temperature needs more force, but makes the metal stronger by work hardening and gives a smooth, accurate finish. See the two sides?

explain.say: Lovely work. Forging also lines up the grain to follow the shape, like wood grain round a bend, which is why forged crankshafts and spanners are tougher than cast ones. Exam tip: thickness times speed is constant in rolling, from volume constancy.

faq.q: What is the difference between hot and cold working?
faq.a: Hot working happens above the recrystallisation temperature, so the metal stays soft and new grains form; it needs less force. Cold working near room temperature hardens the metal and gives better surface finish and accuracy.

faq.q: Why does the strip come out of a rolling mill faster?
faq.a: Volume is constant. When the thickness falls and the width stays nearly the same, the strip must get longer, so it leaves faster in proportion to the thickness reduction.

faq.q: How does a rolling mill reduce thickness?
faq.a: Two rolls turning in opposite directions grip the slab by friction and squeeze it through a gap smaller than its thickness. The biggest reduction per pass is about mu squared times the roll radius.

faq.q: Why are forged parts stronger than cast parts?
faq.a: Forging closes internal voids, refines the grain and makes the grain flow follow the shape of the part, which improves toughness and fatigue strength.
When metal is deformed cold, dislocations multiply and tangle, so further deformation gets harder. The metal becomes stronger and harder but less ductile.

facts: In rolling, thickness × speed stays constant because metal volume is conserved.
The maximum draft per rolling pass is about μ²R.

quiz.say: A strip 6 millimetres thick enters rolls at 2 metres per second and leaves 4 millimetres thick. Its width does not change. What is its exit speed?
quiz.show: Strip 6 mm → 4 mm, entry speed 2 m/s, width constant. Exit speed?

wrong.1: That inverts the ratio; thinner strip must move faster.
wrong.2: The strip gets longer, so it must speed up.

quiz.say: Which is a benefit of cold working?
quiz.show: A benefit of cold working is…
quiz.why: Cold deformation multiplies dislocations, raising strength and hardness.

wrong.1: Cold working needs higher forces than hot working.
wrong.2: Cold-worked metal loses ductility and can crack if pushed too far.
